climbing_route.label: South/southwest talus and scree slopes
climbing_route.notes: Leave the maintained trail at or just below Fortune Creek Pass and angle east/northeast off-trail onto the open talus and scree slopes on the south/southwest aspect of Esmeralda's west (true) summit. Roughly 900-1,100 ft of unmaintained, sustained talus/scree scrambling with some minor route-finding through boulder bands. Watch for rockfall from parties above/below on this loose terrain, lingering snow patches in the gully into early summer (traction/axe useful then), and no water once you leave the basin meadows.

climbing_route.label: Rockier crux band
climbing_route.notes: A rockier crux band partway up is easiest skirted to the west; a boulder-field alternative exists farther west if the direct scree gully is too loose.

climbing_route.label: Fryingpan Glacier to Whitman Notch
climbing_route.notes: Above Meany Crest, gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up here — this begins sustained glacier travel with real crevasse hazard. Climb generally south/southwest across the lower glacier apron to the broad notch separating the Fryingpan and Whitman Glaciers (~9,000-9,100 ft, commonly called Whitman Notch).

climbing_route.label: Upper Whitman Glacier
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, traverse and climb the upper Whitman Glacier, crossing a bergschrund — usually a straightforward step-across early season, wider and trickier late season — up moderate glacier slopes to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to a loose rock-and-scree gully.

climbing_route.label: Gully, headwall step and gully-chimney
climbing_route.notes: Climb the loose rock-and-scree gully to a short (~6 ft) headwall step, then a gully-chimney to the summit notch.

climbing_route.label: Summit ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: An exposed, loose scramble of roughly 30-100 ft along a narrow, crumbly andesite ridge crest to the 11,138 ft summit. There is major exposure here, with a roughly 2,000 ft drop to the Emmons Glacier on the north side; afternoon whiteout or thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.

climbing_route.label: South face and south arete
climbing_route.notes: From the moraine high camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, a roped glacier crossing reaches the base of the peak, where the original 1970 line climbs rock up the south face and south arete. Loose, exposed ground near the high camp is easy to lose in cloud.

climbing_route.label: West face finish
climbing_route.notes: The line finishes on the west face. Route-finding here is the crux in poor visibility, since Ghost Peak, Crooked Thumb, and Phantom Peak all crowd the same skyline.

climbing_route.label: Scree to the saddle on Katsuk's west-summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: From Ragged Ridge Camp, gain a further 200-600 ft to a saddle/bench on the ridge descending from Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short stretch of 4th-class scrambling near the top.

climbing_route.label: Southwest Gully to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: Locate the leftward-trending Southwest Gully high on the peak, which runs up toward a mushroom-shaped summit block. Low in the gully, bypass a waterfall by staying on its left (west) side on loose, 'kitty-litter' scree. In early season (before roughly July) the entire gully holds steep snow to 45 degrees and demands an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing technique.

climbing_route.label: East ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A subsidiary rock knob (Pk. 8165) blocks a direct line up the south side, so the route bends onto the mountain's east ridge — a sustained but pleasant scramble on exposed, blocky granite — to the summit. From the Lake of the Woods camp this final push runs about 2-4 miles round trip with 1,300-1,400' of gain and takes under 2 hours each way for a fit party.

climbing_route.label: Northwest ridge variation
climbing_route.notes: An older, less-used line to the summit follows the northwest ridge from Pistol Pass before cutting southeast, as an alternative to the west-slope/east-ridge line from the Lake of the Woods camp.

climbing_route.label: South face gully
climbing_route.notes: From St. Peter's Gate, most parties cache overnight packs and descend about 300 ft to the base of a basalt cliff, then follow a vague climber's path up the gully on Mt. Stone's south face into a rock bowl below the summit block. Fog is common and has caused parties to lose the route.

climbing_route.label: West ridge to the true summit
climbing_route.notes: Join the standard west-ridge route for a final ~100 ft of scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the true (south) summit.

climbing_route.label: South/southwest gully on the summit tower
climbing_route.notes: The standard line aims for a prominent gully on the south/southwest side of the summit tower, climbed as scree/talus with a bit of low third-class scrambling near the top to gain the final summit block. Often snow-filled into early summer — an ice axe and sometimes light traction are worth carrying outside of peak summer. There is no maintained trail above the lake: expect real route-finding, increasingly loose talus, and a few short cliff bands that force minor backtracking.

climbing_route.label: West ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the unstable lateral moraine at the head of the cirque (loose blocks, exercise care), gain the west ridge and follow it up through talus and blocky olivine to the summit rocks. The rock is famously high-friction but loose in spots; carry water for the dry ridge scramble since Green Creek is the last reliable source.

climbing_route.label: Summit rocks
climbing_route.notes: Short steps near the top; route-finding through several false summits in the upper third is the main crux in poor visibility.
